title: ICSE CLASS 10 — Social Science | Making of Global World Trade
description: Subject-wise test on Making of Global World Trade (Social Science) for ICSE CLASS 10. 50Q.
subject: icse10-sst
instructions: Topic: Making of Global World Trade

questions.question: Which ancient trade route was primarily known for connecting China to the West, facilitating the exchange of goods like silk, spices, and tea?

options.text: Trans-Saharan Route
options.explanation: The Trans-Saharan Route connected West Africa to North Africa and Europe, primarily trading gold and salt.

options.text: Spice Route
options.explanation: The Spice Route was used for trading spices, but it was not primarily focused on connecting China to the West.

options.text: Silk Route
options.explanation: The Silk Route was the primary trade route connecting China to the West, facilitating the exchange of silk, spices, and tea.

options.text: Amber Road
options.explanation: The Amber Road was a trade route for amber, primarily in Europe.

questions.explanation: The Silk Route was a historical network of interlinking trade routes across the Afro-Eurasian landmass that connected East, South, and Western Asia with the Mediterranean and European world, primarily known for the trade of silk from China.
questions.hint: This route was named after a valuable fabric traded extensively.
questions.subject: icse10-sst

questions.question: The repeal of the Corn Laws in Britain during the mid-19th century had which significant economic consequence?

options.text: It led to a sharp increase in the price of food grains within Britain.
options.explanation: The repeal of the Corn Laws allowed cheaper imports, which would lower prices, not increase them.

options.text: It allowed for the free import of cheaper food grains into Britain.
options.explanation: The repeal of the Corn Laws removed restrictions on importing cheaper food grains.

options.text: It encouraged British farmers to increase their domestic grain production significantly.
options.explanation: The repeal of the Corn Laws made it harder for British farmers to compete with cheaper imports, discouraging domestic production.

options.text: It resulted in a decline in the overall demand for food in urban areas.
options.explanation: Cheaper food imports would increase demand in urban areas, not decline it.

questions.explanation: The Corn Laws restricted the import of cheap foreign grain. Their repeal allowed cheaper food imports, which benefited industrialists and urban dwellers by lowering food prices.
questions.hint: The Corn Laws were laws that imposed tariffs on imported grain.
questions.subject: icse10-sst

questions.question: The Bretton Woods institutions, established post-World War II, were primarily designed to achieve which of the following goals?

options.text: To ensure economic stability and full employment in the industrial world.
options.explanation: The Bretton Woods institutions aimed to promote economic stability and full employment globally.

options.text: To promote military alliances against the Soviet Union.
options.explanation: Military alliances were not the primary goal of the Bretton Woods institutions.

options.text: To facilitate the decolonization of African and Asian nations.
options.explanation: Decolonization was not a primary objective of the Bretton Woods institutions.

options.text: To regulate international environmental protection agreements.
options.explanation: Environmental protection was not a focus of the Bretton Woods institutions at their inception.

questions.explanation: The Bretton Woods Conference (1944) established the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank to secure economic stability and full employment in the industrial world, linking national currencies to the dollar.
questions.hint: These institutions were created to stabilize the global economy after World War II.
questions.subject: icse10-sst

questions.question: What was 'Rinderpest', which devastated African economies in the 1890s?

options.text: A new system of forced labour imposed by colonial powers.
options.explanation: Rinderpest was a disease, not a labor system.

options.text: A type of highly profitable cash crop introduced by Europeans.
options.explanation: Rinderpest was a disease, not a cash crop.

options.text: A fast-spreading cattle disease that killed 90% of the cattle.
options.explanation: Rinderpest was a cattle disease that devastated African economies by killing most of the cattle.

options.text: A rebellion by African pastoralists against European encroachment.
options.explanation: Rinderpest was a disease, not a rebellion.

questions.explanation: Rinderpest was a deadly animal disease that arrived in Africa in the late 1880s, brought by infected cattle from British Asia. It spread rapidly, killing up to 90% of cattle in some areas, devastating African livelihoods.
questions.hint: This disease affected livestock and had a severe economic impact on Africa.
questions.subject: icse10-sst

questions.question: How did technological innovations like refrigerated ships impact global trade in the late 19th century?

options.text: They made the transportation of all goods, including non-perishables, significantly more expensive.
options.explanation: Refrigerated ships primarily benefited the transport of perishable goods and did not make all transportation more expensive.

options.text: They led to a decrease in the overall volume of goods traded across oceans.
options.explanation: Refrigerated ships increased the volume of goods traded by enabling the transport of perishable items.

options.text: They enabled the transport of perishable foods like meat and butter over long distances, making them cheaper and more accessible.
options.explanation: Refrigerated ships revolutionized global trade by allowing perishable foods to be transported long distances without spoilage.

options.text: They primarily benefited Asian economies by increasing their export of manufactured goods.
options.explanation: Refrigerated ships primarily benefited Western economies by enabling the import of perishable foods from colonies.

questions.explanation: Refrigerated ships allowed perishable foods like meat, butter, and eggs to be transported from distant farms (e.g., America, Australia, New Zealand) to European markets without spoilage, dramatically changing diets and food prices.
questions.hint: This innovation made it possible to transport perishable goods over long distances.

questions.question: During the Great Depression (1929-1930s), what was a major impact on India, then a British colony?

options.text: India experienced an industrial boom due to increased demand from Britain.
options.explanation: The Great Depression led to a decline in demand, not a boom.

options.text: The prices of agricultural products in India increased significantly.
options.explanation: Agricultural prices plummeted during the Great Depression.

options.text: The British government invested heavily in Indian infrastructure projects.
options.explanation: There was no significant investment in infrastructure during the Great Depression.

options.text: Agricultural prices in India plummeted, severely affecting peasants and farmers.
options.explanation: The Great Depression caused agricultural prices in India to fall sharply, devastating peasants and farmers.

questions.explanation: India's economy was deeply integrated with the global economy. The Great Depression led to a sharp fall in agricultural prices and exports from India, which devastated Indian peasants and farmers who were dependent on cash crops.
questions.hint: The Great Depression caused a significant decline in global trade and prices.
questions.subject: icse10-sst

questions.question: Which of the following was the primary reason for the large-scale migration of Europeans to America and Australia in the 19th century?

options.text: Religious persecution by authoritarian regimes in Europe.
options.explanation: While religious persecution was a factor for some migrants, it was not the primary reason for large-scale migration.

options.text: The desire to establish new colonial outposts for European powers.
options.explanation: Colonial expansion was not the primary motivation for individual migrants.

options.text: The pursuit of better economic opportunities and escape from poverty and hunger.
options.explanation: The primary reason for migration was the pursuit of economic opportunities and escaping poverty.

options.text: Forced displacement due to widespread warfare across Europe.
options.explanation: While warfare caused displacement, it was not the primary reason for large-scale migration to America and Australia.

questions.explanation: Millions of Europeans migrated to America and Australia in the 19th century, primarily seeking new economic opportunities, land, and a better life, often fleeing poverty, disease, and unemployment in their home countries.
questions.hint: The primary motivation was economic in nature.
questions.subject: icse10-sst

questions.question: The 'Group of 77' (G-77) was formed by developing countries in the 1960s with the main objective to:

options.text: Form a military alliance to counter the influence of superpowers.
options.explanation: The G-77 was not a military alliance but an economic coalition.

options.text: Establish a common currency for international trade among member nations.
options.explanation: The G-77 did not aim to create a common currency.

options.text: Demand a New International Economic Order (NIEO) for fairer global trade and control over their natural resources.
options.explanation: The primary objective of the G-77 was to demand a NIEO for fairer global trade and control over natural resources.

options.text: Promote cultural exchange programs between its member states.
options.explanation: Cultural exchange was not the primary focus of the G-77.

questions.explanation: The G-77 was formed by developing countries to challenge the existing unequal global economic order, dominated by Western powers. They demanded a New International Economic Order (NIEO) to gain real control over their natural resources and fairer prices for raw materials in international markets.
questions.hint: This group aimed to reform global economic policies to benefit developing nations.
questions.subject: icse10-sst

questions.question: Assertion (A): By the mid-19th century, British manufacturers were exporting large quantities of cotton textiles to India. Reason (R): The British colonial government in India actively encouraged the growth of indigenous textile industries to meet global demand.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: Assertion A is true, but Reason R is false.

options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: Reason R is false, so this option is incorrect.

options.text: A is true, but R is false.
options.explanation: Assertion A is true, but Reason R is false as the British discouraged indigenous textile industries.

options.text: A is false, but R is true.
options.explanation: Assertion A is true, so this option is incorrect.

questions.explanation: Assertion A is true; British machine-made goods, especially cotton textiles, flooded the Indian market, displacing local production. Reason R is false; the British colonial government's policies were designed to make India a market for British goods and a source of raw materials, actively discouraging indigenous industrialization.
questions.hint: Evaluate the truth of both the assertion and the reason, and whether the reason correctly explains the assertion.
questions.subject: icse10-sst

questions.question: Imagine a farmer in Punjab, India, in the early 20th century, who has shifted from cultivating traditional food grains to growing cotton. He relies on exporting his cotton to Britain to earn income and purchase food for his family. Which of the following global events would have most severely impacted this farmer's livelihood?

options.text: The opening of the Suez Canal, reducing shipping times to Europe.
options.explanation: The Suez Canal reduced shipping times, which would benefit trade, not harm it.

options.text: An increase in the demand for spices from Southeast Asia.
options.explanation: Increased demand for spices would not directly impact a cotton farmer.

options.text: The Great Depression, leading to a collapse in demand and prices for agricultural goods in international markets.
options.explanation: The Great Depression caused a severe decline in demand and prices for agricultural goods, severely impacting the farmer's livelihood.

options.text: The establishment of the Bretton Woods institutions.
options.explanation: The Bretton Woods institutions were established post-World War II and would not have impacted the farmer in the early 20th century.

questions.explanation: The Great Depression (1929-1930s) caused a massive fall in demand and prices for agricultural products globally. A farmer dependent on exporting cash crops like cotton would have faced a severe decline in income, making it difficult to buy food or meet other needs. The other options are either beneficial, irrelevant, or occurred at a time when the impact would be different.
questions.hint: Consider the economic impact of global events on cash crop farmers.

questions.question: Which of the following pre-modern trade routes connected vast regions of Asia with Europe and North Africa, facilitating the exchange of goods, ideas, and culture?

options.text: Trans-Saharan Route
options.explanation: The Trans-Saharan Route connected West Africa with North Africa and the Mediterranean, not Asia.

options.text: Silk Route
options.explanation: The Silk Route connected vast regions of Asia with Europe and North Africa.

options.text: Spice Route
options.explanation: The Spice Route primarily connected Southeast Asia with Europe, focusing on spices.

options.text: Amber Route
options.explanation: The Amber Route connected the Baltic region with the Mediterranean, not Asia.

questions.explanation: The Silk Route is the most prominent example of pre-modern trade routes connecting Asia with Europe and North Africa, playing a crucial role in the exchange of silk, pottery, spices, and cultural elements over centuries.
questions.hint: This route was named after a valuable commodity traded along it.
questions.subject: icse10-sst

questions.question: Which staple food crop, introduced to Europe from the Americas during the Columbian Exchange, significantly improved the diets of the poor and increased life expectancy?

options.text: Wheat
options.explanation: Wheat was already a staple in Europe before the Columbian Exchange.

options.text: Rice
options.explanation: Rice was not a major crop introduced from the Americas.

options.text: Potato
options.explanation: The potato significantly improved diets and life expectancy in Europe.

options.text: Maize
options.explanation: Maize was also introduced but was less impactful on European diets compared to the potato.

questions.explanation: The potato was introduced to Europe from the Americas and became a staple food for the poor, providing a cheap and nutritious food source that helped improve diets and increase life expectancy, particularly in Ireland and parts of Europe.
questions.hint: This crop is often associated with Ireland and is a tuber.
questions.subject: icse10-sst

questions.question: What was the primary consequence of the British government's decision to abolish the Corn Laws in the mid-19th century?

options.text: Increased prices of food grains in Britain, benefiting local farmers.
options.explanation: Abolishing the Corn Laws led to lower prices, not increased prices.

options.text: Encouraged British farmers to increase corn production through subsidies.
options.explanation: The Corn Laws were abolished, removing subsidies and protections for British farmers.

options.text: Allowed cheaper food imports into Britain, leading to industrial growth and urbanisation.
options.explanation: Cheaper food imports reduced living costs and supported industrial growth.

options.text: Led to a significant decline in Britain's global trade dominance.
options.explanation: The abolition of the Corn Laws actually supported Britain's industrial and trade growth.

questions.explanation: The abolition of the Corn Laws allowed cheaper food imports from countries like America and Australia. This lowered food prices in Britain, which in turn reduced the cost of living for workers and freed up income for consumers to spend on industrial goods, thereby supporting industrial growth and urbanisation.
questions.hint: The Corn Laws were tariffs on imported grain.

questions.question: The fast-spreading disease of cattle, Rinderpest, which devastated African livelihoods in the 1890s, was primarily brought to Africa by:

options.text: European missionaries introducing new livestock.
options.explanation: Missionaries did not introduce Rinderpest; it was brought by colonizers.

options.text: Indian indentured labourers arriving with their animals.
options.explanation: Indentured labourers did not bring Rinderpest to Africa.

options.text: Infected cattle imported by European colonizers to feed their invading armies.
options.explanation: European colonizers imported infected cattle, spreading Rinderpest.

options.text: Local African traders exchanging goods across borders.
options.explanation: Local traders did not introduce Rinderpest; it was brought by colonizers.

questions.explanation: Rinderpest was carried by infected cattle imported from British Asia by European colonizers to feed their troops who were invading Eritrea in East Africa. From there, it spread rapidly across the continent, wiping out 90% of the cattle population in some areas.
questions.hint: The disease was introduced by European colonizers for military purposes.
questions.subject: icse10-sst

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the system of 'indentured labour' that became widespread in the 19th century?

options.text: A system where skilled European workers migrated voluntarily to colonies for better opportunities.
options.explanation: Indentured labour involved workers from Asia and Africa, not skilled Europeans.

options.text: A form of slavery where individuals were forcibly captured and transported to work abroad without pay.
options.explanation: Indentured labour was a contract-based system, not outright slavery.

options.text: A contract-based system where workers agreed to work for a specific employer for a fixed period, often in exchange for passage and subsistence.
options.explanation: Indentured labour was a contract-based system with fixed-term employment.

options.text: A system where European companies hired local workers for short-term projects in their home countries with full legal rights.
options.explanation: Indentured labour involved workers migrating to foreign colonies, not local projects.

questions.explanation: Indentured labour involved workers contracting to work for a specified period (typically five years) for an employer in a foreign country, often in exchange for their passage, food, and accommodation. While often exploitative and resembling slavery, it was legally distinct as a contract-based system.
questions.hint: This system involved workers signing contracts for a fixed period in exchange for passage and subsistence.
questions.subject: icse10-sst

questions.question: **Assertion (A):** The Great Depression had a devastating impact on the Indian economy, particularly on agricultural prices. **Reason (R):** As India was a British colony, its economy was closely linked to the global market, and the sharp fall in international agricultural prices directly affected Indian farmers and exports.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: Assertion A is true, and Reason R correctly explains why the Great Depression impacted Indian agricultural prices.

options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: Reason R directly explains Assertion A.

options.text: A is true, but R is false.
options.explanation: Both Assertion A and Reason R are true.

options.text: A is false, but R is true.
options.explanation: Assertion A is true, and Reason R is also true.

questions.explanation: The Great Depression caused agricultural prices to plummet worldwide. As India was a major exporter of agricultural goods and its economy was deeply integrated into the global (and specifically British imperial) system, Indian farmers and peasants suffered immensely due to the sharp fall in demand and prices for their produce, making Reason R a direct and correct explanation for Assertion A.
questions.hint: Consider the economic relationship between India and Britain during the Great Depression.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the significance of the Silk Routes in ancient and medieval times?

options.text: Primarily for the exchange of military technologies between empires.
options.explanation: The Silk Routes were not primarily for military technology exchange.

options.text: Exclusively for the trade of silk from China to Europe.
options.explanation: The Silk Routes facilitated trade in multiple goods, not just silk.

options.text: Facilitated the exchange of goods, ideas, culture, and disease across continents.
options.explanation: This option correctly describes the multi-faceted role of the Silk Routes.

options.text: Only used by European merchants to access Asian markets.
options.explanation: The Silk Routes were used by merchants from multiple continents, not just Europe.

questions.explanation: The Silk Routes were a vast network connecting Asia, Europe, and Africa, facilitating not just trade in various goods (not just silk), but also the spread of culture, religion, technology, and diseases.
questions.hint: Consider the broader impact of the Silk Routes beyond just silk trade.

questions.question: The introduction of which new food crop from the Americas significantly improved the diet of the poor in Europe, particularly Ireland, leading to population growth?

options.text: Maize
options.explanation: Maize was important but not as impactful as the potato for the poor in Europe.

options.text: Potato
options.explanation: The potato was the crop that significantly improved the diet of the poor in Europe.

options.text: Tomato
options.explanation: Tomatoes were introduced but not as a staple food for the poor.

options.text: Groundnut
options.explanation: Groundnuts were not as widely adopted as a staple food in Europe.

questions.explanation: The potato, brought from the Americas, became a staple food for the poor in Europe due to its ease of cultivation and high nutritional value, dramatically impacting population growth, especially in Ireland.
questions.hint: Think about crops introduced from the Americas that became staples in Europe.

questions.question: What was a common characteristic of 'indentured labour' during the 19th century?

options.text: They were highly paid skilled workers migrating voluntarily for better opportunities.
options.explanation: Indentured labourers were not highly paid or skilled.

options.text: They were mostly European workers migrating to America for industrial jobs.
options.explanation: Indentured labourers were primarily from Asia and Africa.

options.text: They were contract labourers recruited for plantation work, often under harsh conditions, with false promises.
options.explanation: This option correctly describes the characteristics of indentured labour.

options.text: They were permanent settlers in new colonies with full citizenship rights.
options.explanation: Indentured labourers were temporary workers with limited rights.

questions.explanation: Indentured labourers were typically poor workers from India, China, and Africa, recruited under contracts often involving deception and leading to exploitative working conditions in colonies like the Caribbean, Fiji, and Ceylon.
questions.hint: Consider the nature of contracts and working conditions for indentured labourers.

questions.question: What was the primary objective of the 'Corn Laws' enforced in Britain during the early 19th century?

options.text: To encourage the import of cheap food grains into Britain.
options.explanation: The Corn Laws restricted imports to protect domestic producers.

options.text: To restrict the export of British manufactured goods.
options.explanation: The Corn Laws were about grain imports, not manufactured goods.

options.text: To protect domestic grain producers from foreign competition by restricting corn imports.
options.explanation: This option correctly describes the primary objective of the Corn Laws.

options.text: To promote free trade in agricultural products across Europe.
options.explanation: The Corn Laws were protectionist, not promoting free trade.

questions.explanation: The Corn Laws were protectionist measures designed to keep grain prices high in Britain, benefiting landowners and aristocratic farmers by limiting the import of cheaper foreign grain.
questions.hint: Consider the economic impact of the Corn Laws on domestic producers and consumers.

questions.question: **Assertion (A):** The Spanish conquest of America was not just a result of superior firepower but also the spread of diseases. **Reason (R):** The native American populations had no immunity against diseases like smallpox brought by the European conquerors.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: Both the assertion and reason are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion.

options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: The reason correctly explains the assertion.

options.text: A is true, but R is false.
options.explanation: Both the assertion and reason are true.

options.text: A is false, but R is true.
options.explanation: The assertion is true, and the reason is also true.

questions.explanation: The devastating impact of diseases like smallpox, to which native Americans had no prior exposure or immunity, decimated their populations, significantly weakening their resistance and aiding the Spanish conquest more than military might alone.
questions.hint: Evaluate the relationship between the assertion and the reason provided.

questions.question: How did the First World War fundamentally alter the global economic balance of power?

options.text: It led to the decline of the US as a major economic power.
options.explanation: The US emerged as a major economic power after WWI.

options.text: It strengthened Britain's economic dominance due to increased war production.
options.explanation: Britain's economic dominance declined after WWI.

options.text: It transformed the USA from an international debtor to an international creditor.
options.explanation: This option correctly describes the economic shift due to WWI.

options.text: It resulted in a long period of global economic stability and growth.
options.explanation: The post-WWI period saw economic instability, leading to the Great Depression.

questions.explanation: During WWI, European powers borrowed heavily from the USA to finance their war efforts. The US economy boomed supplying war materials, leading to its emergence as the world's largest creditor nation and a major economic power.
questions.hint: Consider the economic shifts that occurred due to WWI.

questions.question: Which of the following was a significant factor contributing to the Great Depression in the United States in 1929?

options.text: Massive increase in international trade and exports from the US.
options.explanation: Increased international trade was not a factor in the Great Depression.

options.text: Overproduction in agriculture combined with declining demand and falling prices.
options.explanation: This option correctly identifies a significant factor contributing to the Great Depression.

options.text: Strict government regulation of the stock market preventing speculation.
options.explanation: Lack of regulation, not strict regulation, contributed to the Great Depression.

options.text: A rapid increase in consumer purchasing power and stable employment.
options.explanation: Declining purchasing power and unemployment were factors in the Great Depression.

questions.explanation: Agricultural overproduction in the 1920s led to a glut of produce, falling prices, and farmer debt. This, combined with industrial overproduction and speculative bubbles in the stock market, created an unstable economic environment that eventually collapsed, triggering the Great Depression.
questions.hint: Consider the economic conditions in the US during the 1920s and early 1930s.

questions.question: The Bretton Woods institutions, namely the IMF and the World Bank, were primarily established after the Second World War with which main objective?

options.text: To promote communism and state-controlled economies globally.
options.explanation: The Bretton Woods institutions were not established to promote communism.

options.text: To ensure global peace and security through military alliances.
options.explanation: The Bretton Woods institutions were economic, not military.

options.text: To stabilize the global economy and reconstruct war-torn economies.
options.explanation: This option correctly describes the main objective of the Bretton Woods institutions.

options.text: To facilitate unrestricted free trade between all nations without any regulations.
options.explanation: The Bretton Woods system included regulations to stabilize the global economy.

questions.explanation: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) was established to deal with external surpluses and deficits of member nations, and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD, or World Bank) was set up to finance post-war reconstruction, both aiming for global economic stability and recovery.
questions.hint: Consider the purpose of the Bretton Woods institutions in the post-WWII era.
questions.subject: icse10-sst

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the G-77 is correct?

options.text: It was a group formed by developing countries during the 1960s.
options.explanation: This statement is correct as the G-77 was indeed formed by developing countries in the 1960s.

options.text: Its aim was to demand a New International Economic Order (NIEO).
options.explanation: While this was one of its aims, the question asks for the correct statement, and this is not the only correct one.

options.text: It sought to gain real control over their natural resources and fair prices for raw materials.
options.explanation: This was also an aim, but not the only correct statement.

options.text: It was formed to counter the economic dominance of the Soviet Union.
options.explanation: The G-77 was formed to address economic issues among developing countries, not to counter the Soviet Union.

questions.explanation: The G-77 was formed by developing countries in the 1960s to demand a New International Economic Order (NIEO), gain control over natural resources, and ensure fair prices for raw materials. It was not formed to counter the Soviet Union.
questions.hint: Evaluate each statement carefully to identify the correct one.
questions.subject: icse10-sst

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a major factor contributing to the Great Depression of 1929?

options.text: Overproduction and falling prices in agriculture
options.explanation: Overproduction and falling prices in agriculture were significant factors contributing to the Great Depression.

options.text: Collapse of stock markets worldwide
options.explanation: The collapse of stock markets worldwide was a major factor in triggering the Great Depression.

options.text: Excessive government spending in European countries
options.explanation: Excessive government spending was not a cause of the Great Depression; governments faced debt and austerity instead.

options.text: Decline in international trade due to high tariffs
options.explanation: The decline in international trade due to high tariffs worsened the economic crisis during the Great Depression.

questions.explanation: The Great Depression was caused by factors like overproduction, stock market collapse, and trade decline, but excessive government spending was not a cause—rather, governments struggled with debt and austerity measures during this period.
questions.hint: Consider the economic policies and global events leading to the Great Depression.

questions.question: The Bretton Woods Conference (1944) established which two key financial institutions?

options.text: United Nations and World Trade Organization
options.explanation: The United Nations and World Trade Organization were not established at the Bretton Woods Conference.

options.text: International Monetary Fund and World Bank

options.text: G-20 and OPEC
options.explanation: The G-20 and OPEC were not established at the Bretton Woods Conference.

questions.explanation: The Bretton Woods Conference in 1944 led to the creation of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank to stabilize global economies and promote development.
questions.hint: Think about the institutions formed after World War II to manage global financial stability.

options.text: French

questions.question: Which of the following was a consequence of the ‘Corn Laws’ in Britain during the early 19th century?

options.text: Increased food prices for the poor
options.explanation: The Corn Laws kept food prices artificially high, hurting the poor.
